message.content:
The sea doesn’t have a single, fixed color—it looks different depending on a few key factors:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow water reflects the sky, so it can look light‑blue or even greenish. Deeper water absorbs longer wavelengths (reds, oranges) and scatters shorter ones (blues, violets), giving a deeper, richer blue. |
| **Clarity / Turbidity** | Clear water lets you see the seabed and any underlying colors (sand, algae, coral). Turbid or algae‑rich water can appear green, brown, or even yellowish. |
| **Sunlight & Angle** | The sun’s position changes the hue: at sunrise/sunset the sea can take on pinks, oranges, or purples; midday it’s usually a bright blue. |
| **Surface Conditions** | Calm water shows a more uniform color; waves and wind scatter light, making the sea look lighter or more mottled. |
| **Substrate & Life** | A sandy bottom can give a pale, almost white tint; a rocky or coral reef can add greens, reds, or blues. |
| **Atmospheric Conditions** | Overcast skies can make the sea look grayish or muted; clear skies give a vivid blue. |

So, while we often think of the sea as “blue,” it can range from turquoise and teal to green, gray, or even reddish‑brown, depending on those environmental variables.
